sections.title: One mass, two directions
teaching: A longitudinal oscillation moves a mass along the spring. As the block moves away from its resting position, the spring stretches or compresses and pulls it back. The block keeps moving through the resting position, so the motion repeats.

A transverse oscillation moves the mass across the spring line. The two ends stay fixed while the middle moves above and below that line. The displaced, already tensioned segments pull the mass back toward its resting position.

Both examples complete one cycle every two seconds, or 0.5 Hz. Changing the direction of motion does not by itself change the rate when mass and effective restoring stiffness match. The longitudinal spring has total stiffness K. The two transverse segments contribute half of that effective restoring stiffness each. This is an ideal motion without damping, using small-displacement transverse behavior enlarged for visibility.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate
teaching: The reference system has mass m and effective restoring stiffness K. Its longitudinal and transverse versions have the same 0.5 Hz frequency. Comparing the two directions within each row isolates the direction of motion from the properties that set its rate.

Increasing the mass to 4m while keeping K unchanged makes the mass harder to speed up or slow down. Each cycle takes longer, so frequency falls to 0.25 Hz, half the reference rate. Keeping mass m and increasing effective stiffness to 4K produces a stronger return toward equilibrium and raises frequency to 1 Hz, twice the reference rate.

The same mass–stiffness relation works for both displayed directions. K means total restoring stiffness in the direction of motion. The transverse example obtains it from pre-tension and geometry, so a thicker spring represents increased effective restoring stiffness. Increasing only an axial spring constant while keeping the transverse tension unchanged is a different change. The blocks are idealized as moving without friction or damping.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes
teaching: Two equal masses lie between fixed ends and are connected through three equal coupling elements. The teal mass 1 and orange mass 2 can move together or oppose one another. These are two independent normal modes, which means each coordinated pattern can keep its characteristic shape while oscillating.

In mode 1, both masses move in the same direction at the same time. This is the lower-frequency pattern, set to 0.4 Hz in the model. In mode 2, one mass moves one way while the other moves the opposite way. Their relative motion changes the middle coupling more strongly, and the frequency is higher. Its frequency is √3 times the first, rather than twice the first.

The lower row adds the displacements from both modes at each instant. A mass can move farther when the two contributions point the same way and less when they oppose one another. This combined motion contains both frequencies and has no single normal-mode frequency. The longitudinal and transverse columns use matching effective couplings, and dashed marks identify equilibrium. Display amplitudes are reduced in the combined row so the masses remain distinct.

sections.title: Three masses have three normal modes
teaching: Three equal masses connected through four equal coupling elements between fixed ends have three independent modes. Teal, orange, and purple identify masses 1, 2, and 3. The longitudinal column moves the masses along the spring line, and the transverse column moves them across it.

In mode 1, all three masses move together. The middle mass has the largest displacement while the two outer masses have equal smaller displacements. This is the lowest frequency. In mode 2, the outer masses move in opposite directions and the middle mass remains at equilibrium. In mode 3, the two outer masses move together while the middle mass moves in the opposite direction. This is the highest frequency.

The displayed frequency ratios are approximately 1, 1.848, and 2.414, with the lowest frequency set to 0.32 Hz in the model. Three modes therefore do not mean frequencies of one, two, and three times the lowest. The bottom row adds all three modal motions with equal coefficients. The middle mass stays motionless in pure mode 2, but it moves when the other modes contribute to the mixture.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode
teaching: A chain with N moving masses has N independent modes in the displayed direction. The rows contain one, two, three, four, five, and six masses, so they contain respectively one, two, three, four, five, and six modes. Together the atlas contains 21 animated systems. The empty upper-right region corresponds to modes that do not exist for those smaller systems.

Each row has equal masses, equal effective coupling stiffness, and two fixed endpoints. Moving from left to right within a row adds reversals in the spatial pattern and increases vibration frequency. Mode 1 has the masses moving together. Higher modes divide them into regions that move in opposite directions, with locations of little or no movement between those regions.

Colors identify mode number in this atlas, rather than individual masses. The largest displayed displacement is scaled to match across panels, so the point of comparison is the pattern and rate rather than which drawing looks tallest. The discrete chains generally have frequency ratios that are not whole numbers. The integer harmonic series of an ideal continuous string is a separate case.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics
teaching: Fixing both ends forces displacement to remain zero at each end. The first mode has one half-wave across the length. The next modes fit two, three, four, and five half-waves into that same length. Each added half-wave shortens the spatial pattern and increases how quickly it oscillates.

The five displayed frequencies are 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 Hz. They are consecutive harmonics of a 100 Hz fundamental and include both odd and even multiples. Their actual vibrations are slowed uniformly to one two-hundred-and-fiftieth of the physical rate for viewing, corresponding to displayed rates of 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6, and 2 cycles per second.

The bottom-left string is the sum of all five modes at each instant. A marked point at 17% of the length is the measurement location. The spectrum places frequency in Hz horizontally and amplitude vertically. Its five equal-height peaks identify the five frequencies present in the mixture. Equal peak heights are arranged by the chosen modal amplitudes at this pickup point, rather than being a rule that all strings or all measurement points must obey.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes
teaching: All edges of the rectangular membrane remain fixed while the interior moves above and below its resting surface. Its mode labels describe how many half-wave divisions occur in each of the two surface directions. The five patterns are (1,1), (2,1), (1,2), (2,2), and (3,1). A (1,1) pattern has one broad region, (2,1) divides along one direction, (1,2) divides along the other, (2,2) divides along both, and (3,1) has three divisions along the first direction.

The combined surface adds the five motions. A black pickup point marks where the displacement is measured, at 23% of one side and 31% of the other. The membrane’s side-length ratio is 1.15 in the model. The combined panel uses a smaller vertical scale than the individual-mode panels so the sum fits in its space.

The spectrum uses frequency in Hz horizontally and relative amplitude vertically. The illustration assigns the five modes frequencies of 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 Hz and selects their amplitudes to produce five equal-height peaks at the pickup. Motion is slowed by a factor of 250. Those equally spaced frequencies are an intentional teaching assignment, not the natural eigenfrequencies of this rectangle. The picture supports combining different patterns and reading their spectral components, without establishing that every membrane naturally has a harmonic series.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction
teaching: A scientific theory describes how a system works clearly enough to produce a prediction. Differential equations express how the relevant quantities change. Solving the model gives behavior that can be compared with measurements rather than relying only on a verbal resemblance between systems.

The lecture proposes modeling the vocal folds as a vibrating membrane and predicts evenly spaced harmonic peaks in a measured laryngeal vibration signal. The experimental question is whether the measured signal’s spectrum has that regular frequency spacing. A measurement of laryngeal vibration followed by spectral analysis would test the prediction against the signal.
The prediction concerns the harmonic structure of voiced laryngeal vibration. The assigned membrane animation does not by itself prove that all natural membrane modes have evenly spaced frequencies.
issues: An experiment is proposed, but this page contains no recorded participant data or measured outcome. Do not report that it succeeded from this page alone.
The general membrane-to-harmonic inference in the slide is qualified by the animation’s explicit assigned-frequency caveat.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end
teaching: The bottom endpoint is fixed, so it is a displacement node and stays still. The top endpoint is free, so it is a displacement antinode and moves the most. A mode must satisfy both conditions at once.

The first mode fits one quarter-wavelength between the ends. The next modes fit three, five, and seven quarter-wavelengths. Their displayed physical frequencies are 100, 300, 500, and 700 Hz, which are the odd multiples of the first frequency. Adding a full half-wave, or two more quarter-waves, preserves a fixed bottom and a free top. An even number of quarter-waves would give the wrong condition at the top.

The spectrum has frequency in Hz on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical axis. Equal excitation produces four equal-height peaks when the four-mode mixture is measured at the free end. The motion is shown at one two-hundred-and-fiftieth of its physical rate.

The fixed–fixed and fixed–free demonstrations are separately tuned to a 100 Hz fundamental. Changing only the boundary condition while keeping the same length and wave speed would halve the fundamental when going from fixed–fixed to fixed–free. Matching their 100 Hz fundamentals therefore requires a change of length or wave speed as well.

teaching: The economic example links a theory of changing systems with boom-and-bust cycles. The slide names Woodford’s Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium theory, abbreviated DSGE. Its accompanying illustration labels unemployment with a black line and inflation with a gray line.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency
teaching: Increasing mass lowers frequency when restoring stiffness is held constant. Increasing effective stiffness raises frequency when mass is held constant. A heavier moving part changes its motion more slowly, while a stronger restoring effect returns it toward equilibrium faster.

In a system with several masses, an added mass matters most where the particular mode moves strongly. Adding it near a motionless location has much less effect on that mode. An increase in local stiffness matters most where the material stretches or compresses strongly.

For the standing-wave patterns being compared, locations of greatest motion alternate with locations of greatest local stretching or compression. A location can therefore be sensitive to a mass change in one mode and to a stiffness change in another. The mode’s spatial pattern must be examined before predicting the frequency change.

An N-mass chain has N independent modes in the displayed direction, but its frequencies are generally not exact integer multiples. An ideal continuous fixed–fixed string fits successive whole numbers of half-waves into the same length and has integer harmonics. An ideal fixed–free string fits odd numbers of quarter-waves and has odd-multiple resonances. These are different system assumptions.

sections.title: A local change affects two modes differently
teaching: The highlighted region lies left of the string’s midpoint. Mode 4, labeled 400 Hz, has a broad displaced region there. The material moves strongly, while the local curve is relatively flat. Mode 5, labeled 500 Hz, passes close to its resting line through the highlighted region, with a much steeper spatial change.

Increasing mass in the marked region lowers mode 4’s frequency because that mass participates strongly in its motion. The same mass change has little effect on mode 5 at the locally small-motion position. Increasing local stiffness contributes little to mode 4 at the relatively flat location, but raises mode 5’s frequency where local stretching is strong.

When mass and stiffness both increase there, the dominant effect is therefore a lower frequency for mode 4 and a higher frequency for mode 5. Identifying a point as merely “on the string” is insufficient. The prediction depends on that point’s motion and deformation in each mode.
issues: The highlighted region is left of center. Read its local patterns rather than assuming a central perturbation. The slide presents an idealized local comparison; a finite region can have small effects beyond the dominant ones.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes
teaching: A line of small masses connected by springs represents air along the vocal tract. The left end is fixed and represents the glottal end of the simplified tube, while the right end is free and represents the open lip end. Motion is longitudinal, so the air elements move along the tube rather than tracing the transverse outline of a string.

The upper row is mode 1, the lowest fixed–free air mode and the F1-like resonance. The lower row is mode 2, the next fixed–free mode and the F2-like resonance. In the uniform-tube comparison, mode 2 oscillates three times as fast as mode 1. This matches the first two odd-multiple resonances of a uniform fixed–free system.

The markers locate one-third of the distance from the glottis for /a/, two-thirds for /i/, and the free lip end for /u/. These are locations to compare within each mode. Moving air masses and changing spring spacing identify where local motion or compression is important before a constriction is introduced.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction
teaching: The MRI examples organize vowel articulation by tongue height and front–back position. “dean” is high and front, “Dan” is low and front, “dune” is high and back, “Don” is low and back, and “done” is central. The dark air space changes as the tongue and lips change position.

The added labels identify three useful constriction locations measured from the glottis. The high-front “dean” example has a constriction about two-thirds of the way toward the lips. The “dune” example has a constriction at the lips. The low-back “Don” example has a constriction about one-third of the way from the glottis. The central “done” comparison is labeled “No constriction.”

These are source examples for comparing the vocal tract’s shape with a mode’s spatial pattern. A constriction’s effect depends on where it lies along that pattern, so different vowel shapes can change the first and second resonances in different directions.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode
teaching: A chain with N moving masses has N independent modes in the displayed direction. The rows contain one, two, three, four, five, and six masses, so they contain respectively one, two, three, four, five, and six modes. Together the atlas contains 21 animated systems. Each row has equal masses, equal effective coupling stiffness, and two fixed endpoints. Moving from left to right within a row adds reversals in the spatial pattern and increases vibration frequency. Mode 1 has the masses moving together. Higher modes divide them into regions that move in opposite directions, with locations of little or no movement between those regions.

Colors identify mode number in this atlas, rather than individual masses. The largest displayed displacement is scaled to match across panels, so the point of comparison is the pattern and rate rather than which drawing looks tallest. The discrete chains generally have frequency ratios that are not whole numbers. The integer harmonic series of an ideal continuous string is a separate case.

sections.title: Why fixed–fixed frequencies are integer multiples
teaching: Both fixed endpoints are displacement nodes. Mode 1 fits one half-wave between them, mode 2 fits two, mode 3 fits three, mode 4 fits four, and mode 5 fits five. The same physical length therefore contains progressively smaller half-wave packets.

The packet overlays group corresponding portions of the modes. The first reveal marks packet 1 in all five rows. The second adds packet 2 in modes 2–5. The third adds packet 3 in modes 3–5. The fourth adds packet 4 in modes 4–5, and the fifth adds packet 5 only in mode 5. The first mode has no additional packet after the first reveal because its full length already contains its one half-wave.

With wave speed held fixed in this ideal string, the shorter spatial patterns vibrate faster. The frequency labels are 1 × 100, 2 × 100, 3 × 100, 4 × 100, and 5 × 100 Hz. Their whole-number ratios follow from fitting one, two, three, four, and five half-waves while preserving nodes at both ends. The black internal markers identify the nodes separating packets.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end
teaching: The bottom endpoint is fixed, so it is a displacement node and stays still. The top endpoint is free, so it is a displacement antinode and moves the most. A mode must satisfy both conditions at once.

The first mode fits one quarter-wavelength between the ends. The next modes fit three, five, and seven quarter-wavelengths. Their displayed physical frequencies are 100, 300, 500, and 700 Hz, which are the odd multiples of the first frequency. Adding a full half-wave, or two more quarter-waves, preserves a fixed bottom and a free top. An even number of quarter-waves would give the wrong condition at the top.

The spectrum has frequency in Hz on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical axis. Equal excitation produces four equal-height peaks when the four-mode mixture is measured at the free end. The motion is shown at one two-hundred-and-fiftieth of its physical rate.

The fixed–fixed and fixed–free demonstrations are separately tuned to a 100 Hz fundamental. Changing only the boundary condition while keeping the same length and wave speed would halve the fundamental when going from fixed–fixed to fixed–free. Matching their 100 Hz fundamentals therefore requires a change of length or wave speed as well.

sections.title: Why fixed–free frequencies are odd multiples
teaching: The bottom is fixed and the top is free. Mode 1 contains one quarter-wave between the fixed node and the free antinode. The next modes contain three, five, and seven quarter-waves within the same length. Adding two quarter-waves at a time preserves the different conditions at the two ends.

The overlays count quarter-wave packets in order. Packet 1 appears in all four modes. Packets 2 and 3 appear in modes 2–4. Packets 4 and 5 appear only in modes 3–4. Packets 6 and 7 appear only in mode 4. Their complete stacks contain 1, 3, 5, and 7 packets, respectively.

The frequencies are 1 × 100, 3 × 100, 5 × 100, and 7 × 100 Hz. The second mode is the third harmonic, rather than the second harmonic, because the intervening even-multiple pattern would not have a free antinode at the top. The boundary conditions decide which patterns fit.

sections.title: Why a constriction can raise one formant and lower another
teaching: A constriction bunches air into a smaller region. In the lecture’s perturbation model, that change increases both effective mass and stiffness. The mass effect slows motion, while the stiffness effect strengthens the restoring response to compression.

These two effects do not automatically cancel. Locations that move most strongly alternate along a mode with locations that compress and uncompress most strongly. Increasing mass matters where air must move a lot. Increasing stiffness matters where compression changes are strong.

The MRI comparison changes from a more open central shape to a shape with a back constriction. The prediction depends on where that constriction falls in each mode. The same change can therefore slow one resonance and speed another, allowing the vocal tract’s shape to produce different formant combinations.

sections.title: The source supplies harmonics and the filter shapes their heights
teaching: The glottal source produces the regularly spaced frequencies associated with voicing. The left spectrum places frequency in Hz on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical axis. It contains a comb of equally high source harmonics every 100 Hz, from 100 to 4000 Hz. The equal source heights are part of this schematic comparison.

The vocal tract acts as a filter with resonant regions called formants. Applying that filter changes the heights of the source harmonics. The right spectrum keeps their 100 Hz spacing, but harmonics near a formant become taller and harmonics between formants become smaller. The broad envelope traced by those heights carries the vowel pattern.

The schwa example /ə/ labels F1 at 500 Hz, F2 at 1500 Hz, F3 at 2500 Hz, and F4 at 3500 Hz. The lowest formant supports the largest illustrated group of harmonics, with further groups around each higher resonance. These are schematic source values for the uniform central vowel comparison, rather than fixed values for every speaker.

The reveal first presents the harmonic source and then adds its filtered result. The filter does not replace the source with only four tones. Many harmonics remain present, with their relative amplitudes shaped around the four resonances.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high
teaching: The source spectrum again contains equally spaced, equally tall harmonics every 100 Hz through 4000 Hz. Frequency runs horizontally in Hz and amplitude vertically. Keeping that source unchanged isolates the effect of a different vocal-tract filter.

The /i/ filter has labeled formants at F1 = 300 Hz, F2 = 2300 Hz, F3 = 3000 Hz, and F4 = 3600 Hz. The filtered spectrum has its first strong group very low in frequency and its next group much higher. This is the low-F1, high-F2 pattern associated with the front constriction explanation.

The 100 Hz harmonic positions remain unchanged when the filter is revealed. What changes is their height. Harmonics around 300 Hz become particularly strong, harmonics in the intervening region become weak, and additional groups appear around 2300, 3000, and 3600 Hz. Formants describe resonant regions of the envelope, while the narrow vertical lines are source harmonics. The labeled values belong to this schematic example.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2
teaching: The left spectrum preserves the same 100 Hz harmonic spacing through 4000 Hz. The right spectrum applies a different vocal-tract filter while retaining those source frequencies. Its horizontal axis is frequency in Hz, and its vertical axis is amplitude.

The /a/ formants are labeled F1 = 750 Hz, F2 = 1200 Hz, F3 = 2600 Hz, and F4 = 3500 Hz. Compared with the /i/ illustration, the first formant is higher and the second is lower, bringing the first two resonant regions closer together. Additional peaks in the amplitude envelope occur around the third and fourth formants.

The first formant lies between the source harmonics at 700 and 800 Hz. Nearby harmonics can be strengthened even when a formant is not itself one of the exact harmonic frequencies. The 100 Hz comb stays in place, and its heights sample the new envelope. The vowel changes because that envelope changes, rather than because the harmonics stop being evenly spaced. sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time
teaching: A spectrum gives the distribution of amplitude across frequency at one instant. A spectrogram places many such distributions next to one another over time. The six small spectra represent three successive /i/ examples followed by three /a/ examples.

The spectrogram’s horizontal axis is time increasing to the right, and its vertical axis is frequency from 0 to 4000 Hz. Moving from a spectrum to a spectrogram transfers the spectrum’s horizontal frequency coordinate to that vertical frequency coordinate. A low-frequency spectral peak therefore appears low in the spectrogram, and a high-frequency peak appears higher.

The second reveal maps amplitude to darkness. High amplitude becomes black, medium amplitude becomes gray, and low amplitude becomes white. A tall peak in a spectrum is therefore a dark region at that frequency in the corresponding time slice. The key’s “Amplitude → ink” label identifies this encoding.

The left side is /i/, with low F1 and high F2. During the transition toward /a/, the first dark formant band rises while the second falls. Higher bands continue above them with smaller changes. Stacking the spectra preserves these changing frequency and amplitude relationships, making the vowel transition visible through time.

sections.title: Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify
teaching: With harmonics at 100, 200, 300, 400 Hz and so on, a formant filter can shape the heights of many closely spaced harmonics. In the stated example, F1 is 300 Hz and F2 is 2100 Hz. Several harmonics sample each resonance region, making the broad formant envelope easier to recognize.

With harmonics at 250, 500, 750 Hz and so on, fewer frequencies fall inside a formant region. A resonance may lie between those frequencies rather than at a harmonic line. The source spectrum then gives fewer samples of the same underlying envelope, so a strong isolated harmonic can be mistaken for the position of a formant.

The comparison graphic holds the vocal-tract filter fixed at formants of 300 and 2100 Hz while changing the source spacing to 100, 250, and 350 Hz. Its top row compares the sampled spectra, and its bottom row compares spectrograms for the same vowel. Dense source sampling supports broader visible formant bands, while sparse sampling can make the bands look like isolated harmonic traces. Increasing pitch changes how densely the same filter is sampled.

The surrounding examples extend the issue to a toddler with harmonics at 400, 800 Hz and onward, and a soprano with harmonics at 800, 1600, 2400 Hz and onward. Those values describe separate high-pitch examples. A higher source fundamental does not by itself establish that the vocal-tract formants have risen.
issues: The original comparison graphic is a one-frame 640×360 GIF. Its small explanatory labels have limited resolution. Main labels, values, source/filter conditions, and graphical comparisons were checked against the surrounding native slide text.
